speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Such active mobility devices and new business models for the sharing of these devices have changed the way Singaporeans commute.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In 2017, the House passed the Active Mobility Act (AMA) 2017, which allowed bicycles and PMDs to be used on public paths, including footpaths and cycling paths, and for PABs to be used on cycling paths.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The take-up rate of active mobility devices grew dramatically over the last three years.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These devices provide a cheaper, cleaner and more convenient commuting option.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But as the device population grew, there were concerns about whether our infrastructure and regulatory framework were adequate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: With the amendments in this Bill, only non-motorised active mobility devices, such as bicycles and kick-scooters and PMAs, will be allowed on footpaths.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The exception for motorised PMAs is for the benefit of those who have difficulty walking.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We recognise this connectivity loss for motorised PMD users and we are ramping up our cycling path infrastructure building plans so that Singaporeans can continue to benefit from active mobility devices.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will announce more about these infrastructure plans during the Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Collectively, these two Bills will help us to build a regulatory framework for a safer and sustainable active mobility landscape here in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The two Bills will give us powers to effectively regulate individual active mobility device users, retailers, businesses and device-sharing operators, all of whom have a role to play to ensure public path safety.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The rules and regulations governing user behaviour were developed in consultation with the Active Mobility Advisory Panel (AMAP).

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This body has representatives from seniors, youths, device users and grassroots leaders.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Panel has made further recommendations to strengthen regulations on active mobility device users.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have studied them and announced that we will accept them.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will tighten the regulatory regime for device users in three ways.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: First, we need to ensure that riders are mature enough and have a sufficient understanding of the rules to behave responsibly.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is especially important for riders of motorised active mobility devices, which have the potential to travel fast and cause great harm to others.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will start with e-scooter and PAB riders.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Those who successfully complete the required tests will be issued a competency test certificate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It will be an offence to ride an e-scooter or a PAB on public paths without this competency test certificate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As PABs are also allowed to be used on the roads, PAB riders will similarly be required by the Traffic Police to pass a theory test before they can ride on roads.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Active mobility devices are generally very easy to operate and so we are starting first with a theory test.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is a calibrated approach to improve awareness of rules and regulations while managing the regulatory burden on device users.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If necessary, the Land Transport Authority (LTA) will have the flexibility to introduce other types of tests, such as practical riding tests, in the future.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Under the new section 23G, even if riders have passed the earlier tests, LTA can also require them to take the new tests.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will also introduce a minimum riding age for motorised PMDs, starting with e-scooter riders.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As a general rule, persons under 16 years old will not be allowed to ride an e-scooter on cycling paths.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: While the Act prescribes both a possible fine and jail term if a rider commits this offence of underage riding, these are maximum penalties.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our Courts retain discretion in imposing punishment, having regard to the circumstances of the case and laws, such as the Penal Code and the Children and Young Persons Act (CYPA).

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The only exception to this underage riding provision is if the underage rider is riding under proper supervision by an appropriate supervisor, as recommended by AMAP.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As a start, we will require the supervisor to be at least 21 years old.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For example, if an adult wishes to supervise an underage rider to ride an e-scooter on a cycling path, the adult needs to take reasonable and practicable measures to ensure that the underage rider does not ride in a way dangerous to people or property and abides by the path riding rules as per Parts 3 and 3A of the Active Mobility Act.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will publish some guidelines to educate supervisors on how to properly supervise the underage rider.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Second, we will tackle distracted riding by tightening user behaviour requirements.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Under the new section 22A, it will be an offence to ride or drive any active mobility device or vehicle on a public path while holding a mobile communication device and operating any of the communication device's functions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is already the case today for motorists under the Road Traffic Act (RTA) and we will further extend the RTA to cover all vehicles used on roads, including bicycles.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: A person who is holding and using a mobile communication device may be distracted and may not have both hands on handlebars or steering wheels, both of which affect their ability to effectively control the device or vehicle when it is moving.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will update and clarify provisions to take into account new technological developments in mobile communication devices, such as wearables.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As a general rule, we will continue to allow such devices to be used, so long as the user is wearing the wearable device in accordance with the manufacturer's design while riding.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Third, we will put in place additional measures to ensure that users only use compliant active mobility devices on public paths.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The current registration regime only requires e-scooter owners to declare that their devices are compliant.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: LTA will be rostering e-scooters that are already registered and declared as UL2272-certified for inspections.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: LTA will also periodically call up certified and registered e-scooters for re-inspections every two years to ensure that they remain compliant and are not illegally modified.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will also require active mobility device owners to take extra care to ensure that their devices are not illegally modified.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If an owner had his or her device inspected and certified to be compliant, but the device was subsequently found to be non-compliant while in their ownership, the owner will be presumed, until the contrary is proved, to have either modified the device, or caused the device to be modified.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Most device users are largely law-abiding and ride responsibly.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: However, LTA's enforcement officers detected about 4,900 offences in 2019.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: To send a stronger deterrent message to this group, we will increase the maximum penalties for certain offences.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will generally double the penalties of key user behaviour offences.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Apart from users, retailers must also behave responsibly when advertising and selling active mobility devices.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In 2019, there were 28 instances where retailers were caught for various offences, including displaying and advertising non-compliant active mobility devices.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will tighten this regulatory regime for retailers in three ways.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: First, to complement the mandatory inspection regime for e-scooter owners, we will also require retailers to send e-scooters for inspection to certify that they comply with the prescribed device criteria before they are allowed to register, display, advertise or sell these e-scooters.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Such an arrangement will benefit consumers for an assurance that the e-scooter they purchase is compliant.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will retain the flexibility to extend this to other active mobility devices in future if necessary.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Second, we will strengthen LTA's ability to enforce against illegal modifications.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Today, the controls over illegal modifications only cover modifications done to an active mobility device belonging to another person and done in the course of business.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This means that an individual can circumvent these controls by claiming that he or she is modifying their own device, or is modifying the device as a friend for free.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will expand Part 4 of the AMA to cover all modification activities on active mobility devices that are allowed for use on public paths, whether or not undertaken in the course of business.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is because all illegally modified devices can pose public path safety and fire safety risks.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Third, errant retailers who sell non-compliant active mobility devices have a disproportionately large impact on public path safety.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: To send a strong deterrent message, we will significantly increase penalties for retailer offences.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will also introduce higher fines for corporate entities that cannot be subject to imprisonment.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Hence, for the offence of selling a non-compliant device for use on public paths, we will further double the fine to $40,000 for a first-time offender that is a corporate entity.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Businesses using active mobility devices on paths have a responsibility towards riders and members of the public in the course of their business.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: To provide victims greater recourse to compensation, we will require certain businesses to ensure that their riders are covered by third-party liability insurance for death or bodily injury to any person that the rider may incur when riding on public paths.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will start by imposing this requirement on our device-sharing operators who are licensed under the Shared Mobility Enterprises Bill and businesses which employ or contract with riders who ride active mobility devices on public paths for work, such as food delivery companies.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Our approach is based on AMAP's recommendation to adopt a staged approach, starting first with imposing insurance requirements on certain businesses before extending it to individuals.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are working with AMAP and the insurance industry to study how best to extend such insurance requirements to individual active mobility device riders.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Businesses which provide active mobility devices to be ridden on public paths as part of their business have a special responsibility.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The device-sharing licensing regime, which was established in February 2018 under the Parking Places Act (PPA), focused on tackling indiscriminate device parking, particularly by shared bicycles.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It regulated device-sharing services that operate in public places.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Today, we see a variety of operators using different devices, including motorised ones, causing problems with parking and safety.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For example, there have been operators who provide e-scooters for hire on private land and these devices are subsequently observed on public paths.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Different business models are likely to be developed in the future.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Thus, it is necessary to update our regulatory regime.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This will ensure that operators also play a role in improving the safety of public paths where their devices may be ridden.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It will not matter whether the devices are intended to be parked at public places or not, nor whether the hirers are the general public or only a segment of the public.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Overall, this regime will result in a more comprehensive solution to cover different types of operators, but also allow us to take a calibrated approach to regulate them, depending on their individual characteristics.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: All operators who offer dockless devices for hire will be regulated under the regular licensing regime.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will take a calibrated approach in applying the safety requirements, depending on whether the operators are offering for hire motorised or non-motorised devices.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The current process whereby operators have to demonstrate their ability to meet our regulatory requirements under a sandbox licence before being able to graduate to a full licence, will continue to apply.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As bicycles are non-motorised and pose less of a safety concern, as a start, we will subject dockless bicycle-sharing operators to requirements that deal with parking matters only.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Thus, for now, dockless bicycle-sharing operators regulated under the existing licensing regime will not experience any changes or additional requirements.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is a need to regulate device-sharing operators who offer for hire motorised devices differently from those who only offer for hire non-motorised devices because of the increased risk of harm to the rider and to the public.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Presently, there is a Ministerial safety directive in force under PPA, as a result of which LTA does not issue any licences to PMD-sharing companies and does not accept new applications for PMD-sharing licences.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Moving forward, LTA will continue to assess the public path safety situation and the readiness of the industry when assessing licence applications by those who offer motorised device-sharing services.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Appropriate safety requirements will be imposed if licences are granted for this group, which may include ensuring that the motorised devices are equipped to accurately identify the device location and travelling speed, and ensuring that the devices only operate in limited geographical spaces specified by LTA.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: LTA will also be able to require operators to ban users who have committed serious offences from using their shared devices.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Class licensees do not need LTA's explicit periodic approval to operate, and only need to register with LTA soon after commencing operations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Class licensees will also be subjected to a smaller set of regulatory requirements, such as installing speedometers on their active mobility devices.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This light-touch approach is because these docked operators, such as those who operate from a physical shopfront or who have built racks where their devices are affixed to, cause less parking disamenities due to their use of docking infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They generally have to incur higher initial infrastructure costs, which naturally restrict the scale of their operations and, correspondingly, their safety impact.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Notwithstanding this, LTA will have the flexibility to shift such operators into the regular licensing regime subsequently, if there is a need to do so.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Even for docked device-sharing operators, we will take a calibrated approach.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As a start, we intend to apply the class licensing regime only to docked device-sharing operators using motorised active mobility devices, and not to those using non-motorised devices which have fewer safety concerns.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Therefore, as a start, docked bicycle-sharing operators will not be required to have a regular licence or a class licence.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Nonetheless, LTA will have the powers to impose the licensing regime on them as necessary.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are aware that this class licensing regime will apply to some existing and currently unlicensed operators and will engage these operators further to discuss the implementation details and to provide sufficient transition time.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We aim to minimise compliance costs and make the registration process easy.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, with regard to the assessment tests, I would like to propose that LTA build upon the existing training the "Delivery Rider Kit".

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This was curated by the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) in consultation with the food delivery platforms.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It will support PMD delivery riders transiting to other modes, such as PABs.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The topics that we have included comprise safe riding, using PABs effectively, digital skills and so on.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More recently, Minister Khaw Boon Wan also attended one of these training sessions.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We feel that there should be some alignment between the new assessment test and the NTUC's Rider Kit.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Food delivery riders who have attended the training have also given us very good feedback and they are happy with the contents of the training.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that they would not need to attend additional classes or to be re-assessed if they have completed those training sessions.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The practical assessment and the knowledge learnt during these existing courses are substantial and useful.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On top of that, GrabFood offered its food delivery riders who have completed the safe riding module a safety helmet which has a smart lights feature.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The lights help increase their visibility while they are on the road and also serves as turn signals for other motorists to note when these riders are making turns.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How great it is if all other food delivery operators also do the same and equip their riders with similar helmets.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope the Ministry can lend its weight to effect that outcome when they are in dialogues with the other food delivery platforms.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One other area that we are concerned with and we should pay attention to is whether the riders are exhausted from working long hours or rushing from place to place because of the incentive structure.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many may be working long stretches or trying to hit targets to meet the incentive payouts.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The use of, for example, telematics or data analytics, could offer options to promote safer rides.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This industry currently is a piece-rate kind of industry structure.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The more you do, the more you earn.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When you hit a certain target, you get higher incentives.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such a scheme may not exactly be safe for the riders because regardless of their health or the status of their exhaustion, they may try to push for higher targets.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We hope to hear perhaps another way of addressing this issue rather than let the existing business model continue on, which may affect the riders in a negative manner.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That is a move in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is, however, not mandatory for them to provide accident or prolonged medical leave insurance for their rider partners.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some do so, but the majority are not on board yet.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Both business models are fairly similar – one, providing point-to-point service for commuters, the other, providing point-to-point service for food delivery.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are there plans to work with the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) to look at potential employment-related insights?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It will be useful to deepdive into whether there may be issues of skills mismatch among the riders.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Are they in this job because of circumstances, such as this being a low entry barrier job so anybody can actually enter in without an interview or such other consideration?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Or could it be that there is instant cash payout and the incentive scheme in the job attractive?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Or could it be that our skills conversion programme may not be effective in helping people land a job and, consequently, they end up delivering food as a mode of making a living?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There could be some fundamental issues here as to whether are there too many workers in this industry or is it a sustainable career for those who have opted for this industry?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Do they have adequate Central Provident Fund (CPF) savings?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And what are the skillsets needed to help those who wish to transit into a new sector, into a new job?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Have we been able to do so effectively?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These are areas in which perhaps LTA may not have the full range of skillsets or the tools but it would be useful to work with MOM to ensure that workers are assessed appropriately to help them and guide them in their appropriate career option.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Regardless, Mr Deputy Speaker, the amendments are a step in the right direction as far as regulations are concerned.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some businesses are responsible and have taken positive acts.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Since then, I have received fewer complaints from residents about reckless riders, and my residents have generally expressed support for the ban.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am pleased to note that other motorised mobility devices like electric hoverboards and unicycles will also be banned from footpaths progressively by March.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure this was a difficult decision to make, in light of those who depend on PMDs for their livelihood and also when we are trying to move towards a car-lite nation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, as I have said not once, not twice but many times in this House, something had to be done, given the casualties, injuries, near-misses caused by reckless e-scooter users, besides the fires caused during battery charging.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Human lives must be prioritised above everything else.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is only after taking care of that that we can explore new solutions.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I note that a number of regulations have also been introduced to improve safety with regard to riding of PMDs on public paths.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This is great and I, too, have been calling for a minimum age and for users to partake in a qualifying assessment before they can hit the paths.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How many registered users are there currently and how long will this take to be rolled out?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Will those who passed the test be issued certification or a licence that they have to carry with them when riding?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am also concerned about the limitations of the regulations.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Multiple people in a household may share a device.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some of them may use the device without taking the test and this will likely go undiscovered until they get into an accident.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This problem is likely to be more prevalent among minors.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Children under 16 can illegally use the devices belonging to their older family members.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How can we ensure that there is effective enforcement?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Further, how would these regulations apply to PMD and e-bike rentals?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I suppose customers are required to produce their certificate before they can hire a PMD.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But what about tourists and other foreign visitors who would not have taken the test?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And on the subject of age, would there be any age limit for seniors to ensure that they are medically fit to ride PMDs?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Weak eyesight or other medical problems may cause them to misjudge distances and navigate obstacles safely on the path, which could cause them to endanger themselves and others.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Motorists above 65 are required to undergo a medical check-up every three years by a registered doctor if they want to continue driving.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Would something similar be extended to PMD riders as well?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the latter case, does the responsibility of insurance lie with the employee or the employer?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As with many PMD riders who work with delivery companies, they are not full-time staff.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: With third-party insurance in place, what protocols should be observed in case of an accident?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is the PMD rider required to have a copy of the insurance certificate on him so he can give it to the victim to claim against him?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Even with these measures, any accident is one too many.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Riders who ride recklessly and go beyond legal speed limits still cause a hazard to themselves and all other users.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Does LTA have the resources to catch them and enforce penalties, be it whether they are riding recklessly on path connectors or roads or on footpaths which they are not supposed to?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: On the eve of New Year, when I was on my way to a countdown event at Khatib, I saw a convoy of e-riders happily cruising down along Yishun Avenue 2, as if the whole road belonged to them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I can sympathise, I can appreciate the frustration of the enforcement officers and, in fact, many of my residents expressed sympathy to the enforcement officer who was terminated because he showed his kicking power recently.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Also, many residents shared with me that they feel so unsafe when they are waiting for buses at the bus stops.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Next, let me move on to the issue that more PABs and bicycles could bring.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Is the Ministry sufficiently equipped to monitor the impact of more PABs and bicycles on the roads?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Riding on the roads can be dangerous and I wonder if there are plans to implement mandatory safety courses and tests for all riders.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the past months, cyclists have died after being hit by cars.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There was also one fatal case involving a pedestrian killed by a cyclist.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Frankly speaking, I am really worried about having more cyclists on the roads.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are there incidents of drunk riding on the roads?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the United Kingdom (UK), one can be fined up to £1,000 for riding under the influence of alcohol.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Are there similar laws for cycling in Singapore?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Drunk cycling is a hazard for cyclists, pedestrians and also motorists.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, because of all those fire cases that happened with charging of PMDs, I would like to ask what is being done to ensure that PABs meet fire and electrical safety requirements?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The amendments to the Bill will make our paths safe again.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Of course, we also need the cooperation of every motorist and pedestrian to stay alert and stay on the right paths.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: No matter what regulations we have, PMD speeding still poses a big danger.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government can do more about it.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the many unsafe or inconsiderate e-scooter incidents may reduce for now, let us not forget the painful lessons we have learnt in the past few years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In my speeches on e-scooter issues in the Second Reading of the Active Mobility Bill in January 2017, the Second Reading of the Land Transport (Enforcement Measures) Bill in September 2018 and the Committee of Supply debates for MOT in 2016, 2018 and 2019, I have, among other issues, brought up the following points.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, we have had a poor cycling or riding culture over the years – bicycles beating red lights, cycling against the traffic and, until the AMA came into force, cycling on footpaths.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These acts could be seen on an everyday basis.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not sure even now it has improved in the past three years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, our poor cycling culture coupled with the lack of enforcement by the authorities over the years and the lack of political will of past Governments to improve the riding culture, meant that in recent years, with the introduction of e-scooters, we need to create from scratch a new culture of safe and considerate use of bicycles and PMDs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Three, there must be sufficient public education and consistent effective enforcement, especially early on after the introduction of the new Active Mobility regulations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There must be sufficient resources and a willingness from all authorities concerned responsible for enforcement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government must ensure that information is made available not just to people who voluntarily look for it by way of voluntary Safe Riding courses or on the LTA website or Facebook page.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government must think of how to push such information to both riders and non-riders, such as pedestrians, and to people who do not seek it, and such efforts can be not just in English, but should also be in other languages, such as Chinese, Malay and Tamil.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the completion of the extended cycling network may possibly allow PMDs or e-scooters a new leash of life again, we should not be lulled into thinking that the new cycling lanes with a more extensive network alone will avoid all the problems we have seen with e-scooters in the past three years leading up to its footpath ban.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Most of these problems, I submit, had to do with a poor riding culture, inadequate public education and even inadequate enforcement.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should resolve these issues or problems before the extended cycling path network is ready for use.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Otherwise, the Government will just be kicking the can down the road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For a start, will the cycling paths be directly linked to every Housing and Development Board (HDB) block, condominium, private landed house, shophouse, office building and industrial building?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It cannot be a half-hearted attempt, for example, having cycling paths circling a number of HDB blocks but with no direct link from each block or having cycling paths circling around clusters of private residential estates, expecting e-scooter users to alight and push en route to cycling paths.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If this seem too expensive, impractical or ambitious, then MOT may have to reconsider e-scooters and other PMDs as a serious option for first and final mile connectivity.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, if our cycling path network were to become sufficiently extensive such that PMD riders do not need to alight and push, it may, in turn, do away with the need for cyclists to share the use of footpaths, which is still currently allowed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This prospect may be welcomed by many footpath users who are still not comfortable with the sharing of footpaths with bicycles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If there is no direct link, the existing footpath ban will mean that e-scooter users technically have to alight and push their e-scooters when on roads or footpaths.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How confident are we that all riders will comply accordingly?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the issue of enforcement, while I appreciate the efforts of many LTA enforcement officers, since the AMA took effect, spot checks on certain days of the week or in selected areas may not be adequate.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: People may take their chances and continue to use their devices illegally or in unlawful ways if they think that the chances of meeting enforcement officers are slim.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even now, I still see e-scooters being ridden on the roads or on footpaths, almost every day.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I still see illegal specs e-bikes or PABs on footpaths as well.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And I still see many illegal specs e-bikes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the issue of public education, as I have mentioned earlier, we also need to embark on public education that pushes the education to people of all ages, riders or otherwise, including for those who do not voluntarily seek the information.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I know that Senior Minister of State Lam Pin Min answered my question then by saying that a mandatory theory test would be more appropriate than a safe riding course.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While I do not agree that it should be confined to a mere theory test, certainly, some form of mandatory tests should be introduced, together with disqualification rights.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In November 2019, the Senior Minister of State did not comment on disqualification rights but I believe that, with disqualification rights, people will take greater care to use their e-scooters safely and considerately, so I would urge MOT to incorporate disqualification rights in the proposed regulations.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to ask the Senior Minister of State whether there will be clearer requirements to be spelt out in the subsidiary legislation for such supervisors and the conditions for such escorts?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am also concerned that if there are insufficient LTA enforcement officers in every location, how do we ensure all escorts and supervisors are compliant with the law?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, why do we not only allow all riders to learn after they have reached the statutory legal age for the use of e-scooters, just like how we do with motorcycles, cars and other vehicles on the roads?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will it be the underage rider or the supervisor?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will insurance be made compulsory for all such riding by underage riders?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would also like to touch on an issue regarding e-scooter battery quality.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In closing, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, if the Government still expects e-scooters to be a viable option for first and final mile connectivity when the cycling path network is expanded, I urge the Government to address the issues and concerns I have highlighted and get things right ahead of the expanding cycling path network.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Well, as the joke goes, we all do have access to a BMW – Bus, Mass Rapid Transit (MRT), Walk.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Our extensive and ever-growing public transportation network is certainly making us more mobile, and walking is a key dimension of active mobility.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I would, therefore, like to take this opportunity to speak about walking and walkability, as this Bill introduces timely measures to help pedestrians, cyclists and PMD users share our paths safely.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Providing dedicated lanes for transport modes with speeds between those for walking and for cars is necessary.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: But another critical need is to effectively integrate these cycling paths into our urban landscapes so that pedestrians and cyclists can all benefit.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Since we will be actively expanding our cycling path networks, I would like to suggest an active incorporation of design considerations that take into account the needs of pedestrians.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: To this end, let me draw on research on designing walkable neighbourhoods in Singapore.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: They found that in HDB estates, apartment blocks have principally been developed for the use of cars where precincts are often surrounded and divided by wide, car-based corridors that impede greater active mobility.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: So, even though pedestrians are usually able to make their way from departure point to destination, walking is made cumbersome because of frequent traffic lights along the route or the need to use ramps and overhead bridges to cross a street.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: For example, crossing a road often involves the need to take a long detour and use overhead bridges or a ramp instead of covering the shortest possible route.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Other studies have also found that many HDB estates and new towns have a car-centric design with wide car-oriented corridors that cut into their urban fabric.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: They argued that space and time for crossing are not equally distributed between cars and pedestrians, and that traffic priority is always given to vehicles.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Also, block units are surrounded by parking areas and leftover spaces.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: The consequence of this car-centric approach to our urban design is that active mobility is not ideally facilitated and may, in fact, be undermined due to disruptions and lack of continuity of walking.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Adverse consequences, such as jaywalking, may, therefore, result.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Another issue previous research has identified is the lack of consistent and well-defined urban block planning, because HDB blocks are not homogeneous or consistent but differ in size, design and pattern.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, this makes spatial awareness and navigation more challenging.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Each apartment block is surrounded by parking areas and internal car-based streets that reduce the compactness of each neighbourhood.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Zhang and his co-authors found that the overriding feeling when walking through an HDB neighbourhood is the unnecessarily meandering trips required to reach a destination.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: This is due to the lack of continuity of walking and fragmentation of our urban fabric.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Given all these characteristics of older HDB neighbourhoods, they are clearly not as pedestrian-friendly as they can or should be.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Active mobility is sacrificed for vehicular traffic, thereby making our HDB estates less navigable.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: This has adverse implications not just for pedestrians but also for the wheelchair-bound and young families using strollers and prams.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: But we can draw critical lessons from such research as we design our new HDB estates, and build our expanded cycling network.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, human factors must also be taken into account in boosting active mobility.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Research by Assoc Prof Lynette Cheah and her team at the Sustainable Urban Mobility Research Laboratory in the Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD) has probed into the values that most influence people's choices for active mobility.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: They also established that individuals' experience of travelling on different travel modes also acts as feedback that reshapes their values and perceptions toward current mobility options and expectations for future mobility.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: What this means is that if walking can be convenient, promote physical exercise and offer time and cost savings, individuals will be more likely to incorporate more walking into their mobility patterns.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Conversely, an adverse experience from navigating a meandering and fragmented urban landscape will deter them from walking as much as could be possible or desirable.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I urge our planners to take walkability into account even as they plan the extended cycling pathways, to ensure that these pathways are optimally integrated into our urban landscape and that they do not intrude into or undermine the needs of pedestrians.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Along the same vein, I would like the Ministry to consider if third-party insurance would be useful for all riders.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is to ensure that all victims, not just those involved in accidents caused by business-related riders, can seek recourse and compensation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It would be also helpful if the Ministry can work with insurance firms to ensure affordability.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I would like to comment on the amendment to address the issue of underage riding of PMDs on public paths.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I support those who are underage riding under supervision, there are risks and challenges associated with the control of these machines.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Next, I would like to comment on the amendment to address the issue of underage riding of PMDs on public paths.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I support those who are underage riding under supervision, these are, nonetheless, motorised devices and there are definitely risks and challenges associated with the control of these devices.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): Sir, I would like to conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is safe to say that our journey with "active mobility" has not been a smooth one for our policymakers nor our people since it was first mooted in the Land Transport Master Plan 2013.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It was merely three years ago when bike-sharing was all the rage.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This House had to pass the Parking Places (Amendment) Bill in March 2018 to legislate licensing, restrict fleet size and mandate geofencing.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Now, we rarely see these shared bikes around even though we still have three operators remaining.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Then, came the next micro mobility revolution with e-scooters.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Even more accessible than bicycles given that no special skills are required, their popularity grew due to low barrier to entry, but so did the public scrutiny and outrage with accidents and fire incidents ravaging homes from charging.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Regulations continue to mount to respond to policy gaps that were uncovered with time.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The faith on the readiness of importers, delivery companies, riders and pedestrians to be gracious and responsible participants may now seem misplaced.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The gaps and patch fixes in reaction to challenges over such a short space of time have made both these policy endeavours seem clumsy at best in design and execution.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: So, first, Mr Deputy Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister what have we learned from the many potholes and patch fixes along this journey?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: What about our current models of policy formulation and implementation?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Do we need to update and adapt because bike-sharing and PMDs will not be the only disruptions coming our way?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Asking these questions is not questioning the intention and dedication of our Public Service at all.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is bridging an open dialogue between those who serve and the ones who are served.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Former Head of Civil Service, Peter Ong, once said that the best policy is only as good as its execution.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: He also said that there should be no artificial divide between policy formulation and policy implementation, that there should be ownership of policy design to accountability of "how the policy is translated into outcomes that eventually reach our citizens".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: He emphasised paying attention to details as a key element to improve ability to convert policy formulation into successful execution, even calling the "culture of mastery over details" as one that the Singapore Civil Service is well-known for.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The announcement of the overnight ban of PMDs on footpaths in response to a Parliamentary Question sent shockwaves through the PMD rider community, especially thousands of Singaporeans who are not merely recreational riders but subsist with PMDs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It appeared that this segment of our citizens may have been blatantly marginalised during policy formulation and implementation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Previous policy shifts were progressively implemented but this overnight ban was seen by many as "blunt and rigid" and not well supported with an inter-Ministry response.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Efforts were made by ground-up groups to link them up to ComCare but there was a week's wait to process the application.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Sengchiy finally switched to an e-bike towards end-November but is having trouble adjusting to riding on the road as he is afraid for his own safety.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: So, he switched to only late night hours.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Seline's family is not the only one affected that I know of.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Given that they are the stakeholder most negatively impacted, the grievances of many riders who depend on the PMDs for their work and subsistence could have been mitigated if they were directly consulted before the ban and not just through the delivery companies.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While the ban may have proceeded regardless, the consultation would at least afford these PMD riders a platform to be heard and to offer alternative policy recommendations for the Government's consideration.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, such consultation would also be a good opportunity for the Government to understand and listen to suggestions of different measures which can be put in place to mitigate the negative impact suffered by these PMD riders, so that such measures can be announced alongside the ban.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: As we aspire towards "Singapore Together", the Government must consistently allow stakeholders to participate and be empowered.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, I do acknowledge that the intent with the public consultation exercise and AMAP was well-meaning and certainly a step in the right direction in participatory policymaking.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I note that there was only a representative from the PMD user community on AMAP but it is not immediately clear to me if he or others represent the interests of riders who use PMDs for livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is also not clear to me, Mr Deputy Speaker, if we had considered the behavioural impact on safety relating as a result of the reward algorithms of delivery companies.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: If I am rewarded to make as many delivery trips as I can within the shortest possible time, then I would naturally be in a rush and possibly also tired all the time.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Safety – mine and others – is almost certainly going to be compromised.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: So, we cannot exclude these companies' responsibility in our policy formulation and implementation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This may be the level of details we have to pay more attention to and get better at as we strive to keep up our regulation with innovation and inclusion.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I would like to caution that we must not narrow our active mobility conversation to just that of riders against the rest of the society.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, riders seem to be vilified with these two Bills, including underage riders.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Clause 25 empowers LTA to refuse further to hire vehicles to particular individuals.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Clause 26 further empowers the Minister to issue safety directives without giving the affected person an opportunity to be heard.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While the Trusted Data Sharing Framework was introduced in June 2019 to enable the digital economy, I question the usage of data sharing between licensees to create a list of banned individuals.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Such systematic targeting could lead to unconscious discrimination of certain groups within our society and will degrade our social compact.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Such a policy could leave these individuals unprotected also by rogue licensees.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It was only in October last year that the amended CYPA defines a "young person" as below 18, to better protect our children and to be consistent with the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Under section 37 of CYPA, there are clear restrictions on punishment of children and young persons and it clearly states that they should not be ordered to be imprisoned for any offence.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister please explain why we are passing new laws that go against existing laws, possibly constituting legislative conflict?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I strongly believe in protecting our children and young persons, including their legal rights.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, I would like to ask the Minister to consider commensurate measures, other than imprisonment, for a child or young person found guilty of underage riding of PMD on shared paths.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Should there not be warnings issued and reformative training actions considered before we impose such inappropriate punitive measures on children?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: With these amendments, what measures will the Ministry put in place to better train our enforcement officers in approaching the situation on the ground to avoid tension and skirmishes?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We have a worthy and yet ambitious goal of having 90% of our peak hour trips completed by walking, biking, public transit and shared mobility by 2040.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, these bumps on the road towards active mobility have unfortunately served to narrow our perspectives, putting much of our attention on multiple users with conflicting needs – pedestrians, cyclists and mobility riders – sharing our narrow footpaths, which is, if I may remind everyone, all of 1.5-metre wide.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It really should not come as a surprise at all that tensions and accidents would result.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Albert Einstein said, "We cannot solve the problem with the same way of thinking that created it in the first place".

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: So, instead of going at it as a battle against inconsiderate use of a limited space, how can we expand that physical space beyond the current 1.5 metres so that there is more room for more equitable and safer use by all users, including our car drivers?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Instead of slapping more regulations each time we wish to change behaviours, how can we invest the same, if not, more effort, to build an informed, gracious and adaptive citizenry in an increasingly disruptive environment which must include the most vulnerable amongst us?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Minister Khaw Boon Wan made the promise to return safe footpaths to Singaporeans and he delivered them.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I, therefore, welcome the amendments to AMA and the incorporation of recommendations by AMAP led by Assoc Prof Faishal Ibrahim.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I had on numerous occasions in this House asked the Ministry to consider the licensing of users, compulsory safety training as well as third-party liability Insurance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I am glad that AMAP has made similar recommendations which the Ministry has adopted.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is a point I wish to continue to push for.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While it is undeniable that the vast majority of users constitute those working in the food delivery industry, the remaining number of personal users of PMDs and e-scooters is not small either.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It would, therefore, be important to ensure that before the next spike in number of users occurs when shared paths are completed that comprehensive and affordable TPLI be made available and made compulsory for all users.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With regard to testing, I seek the Ministry's clarification on which companies or agencies will be appointed to do the certification and when can certification begin and end.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: On a related point, with the Shared Mobility Enterprises Bill controlling and licensing shared mobility services, how does the Ministry intend to police the users of the shared devices, such as in ensuring that they have completed competency testing, and how will the law apply to tourists?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Lastly, I wish to seek an update from the Ministry on two additional matters.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A fire was reported involving a PMD battery inside a living room.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Battery was brought out to the corridor by the owner.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Fire was extinguished by the Singapore Civil Defence Force.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Walls on the corridor sustained soot damage, no evacuation was required, paramedic assessed, no conveyors.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Thankfully, no one was seriously injured in this instance and the fire was not extensive.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While I hope this is a rare occurrence since the ban was put in place, we must never leave things to chance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The first reference in British legislation to motorised road transport is the Locomotive Act 1861 which dealt with early steam-powered motor vehicles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Drivers of motor vehicles in the UK were only required to be registered and licensed with the Motor Car Act in 1903.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That may not sound alarming until you find out that driver’s licence testing only became a requirement with the Road Traffic Act 1934.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The Motor Car Act 1903, in fact, allowed licences to be issued to any driver aged 17 and above, unless that driver was specifically disqualified due to having committed an offence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Existing licences, moreover, were grandfathered by the Road Traffic Act 1934.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The point is that we should not be embarrassed that it has taken Singapore a few years to improve on our regulation of new motorised PMDs and services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It took the UK 73 years to deal with motor cars, or maybe 31 years if you are just counting from the Motor Car Act onwards.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And, of course, it took cities decades to upgrade their road infrastructure from being suited for horses, to being safe for cars and people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The fact is that neither the public transport system nor private motor cars are ideal for many short distance trips in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The public transport system struggles to fill the first and last mile cost effectively, and is very expensive to operate for low-demand routes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Private motor cars cause congestion, and have high environmental costs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, active mobility devices are potentially a better, more sustainable means of travel.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I want to commend the Government for consistently articulating a farsighted vision of shared and active mobility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But moving to realise this vision involves costs and benefits to stakeholders, such as pedestrians and existing road users.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: As we have seen, these concerns are expressed very vocally, and this Bill represents an effort to respond to their concerns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There has been a strong and consistent narrative to our efforts to regulate active mobility over the years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We all believe that a culture of gracious and responsible usage of active mobility devices is necessary for such transport innovations to flourish and co-exist with pedestrians and motorists.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There are vast differences between countries in road accident rates, despite similarities in vehicle technology, safety regulations, and driver licensing requirements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Part of the difference is due to motorist and pedestrian behaviour which we can call culture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But there are also fundamental limitations to the role of culture in the transport system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Culture does not replace a functioning system of liability insurance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Culture does not create spaces for people to pass safely on a footpath that was not designed for two-way travel on active mobility devices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Culture does not ensure that vehicles are adequately engineered for safety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If we are not careful, highlighting the role of culture too much becomes a shortcut to magical policy thinking: the belief that we can achieve our policy objectives without considering difficult trade-offs and convincing the public to accept them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The fundamental trade-off in transport safety regulation is between speed, safety and personal autonomy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Faster modes of transport mean safety will be compromised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Improvements to both speed and safety can only be achieved with restrictions on personal autonomy: who is allowed to travel, and how they do it – regulating equipment, design, legally enforceable rules of behaviour.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Culture does allow us some room to boost both speed and safety at once.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We were perhaps initially overly cautious about imposing rules on motorised active mobility devices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We did not want to compromise the very qualities that attracted users: low costs, simplicity, flexibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: After all, bicycles are only very lightly regulated, and have been so for over a hundred years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the case of bicycles perhaps led us to underestimate the capacity of active mobility devices to cause harm and for that harm to be uncompensated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Safety concerns about new transport again are not novel.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The earliest motorised vehicles in the UK were subject to the Locomotive Act 1865.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That Act required a man waving a red flag to walk before any motor vehicle – to protect pedestrians and horses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Safety regulations for motorists obviously have evolved since then.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In case an active mobility device does cause harm, a common law right of tort has always existed to provide redress, just as it does for any harm a pedestrian might cause another on a footpath.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But we have come to realise that relying on this right alone is insufficient because liability is limited by wealth, and legal costs can be considerable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is more efficient to mandate insurance coverage as a way of ensuring uncompensated harm is minimised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The duration of insurance could be commensurate with certification requirements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The insurance system does not need to be designed as a direct to consumer market.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We could have insurers contract with LTA to provide coverage and then collect fees for insurance at registration.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I looked at the debate on the Active Mobility Bill 2017.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, the importance of those suggestions has been borne out by events.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think most would agree that we should not judge our active mobility policy on whether better decisions could have been made with hindsight, but on whether those decisions were the best possible with what was known at that time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I find it hard to say any of us could have done much better in managing active mobility device risks and the fallout on delivery workers, businesses and ordinary users, from the active mobility device footpath ban.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is because there is simply little publicly available data and research in the local context that would have allowed the decision maker at the time to foresee the challenges and risks arising from their policy choices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, the weakness is really in the research and knowledge infrastructure that needs to exist for us to make better decisions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Consider the basic question motivating much of our regulatory effort.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But what is the magnitude of these risks, relative to other types of travel?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Some data has been released in a response to a Parliamentary Question I filed in November 2019 on accidents involving PMDs treated at our hospitals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, are PMDs more or less dangerous than bicycles, which are much less controversial?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: One serious limitation of the data is that we know little about actual travel using these devices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Without travel, we cannot calculate the real risks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, we may find that motorised active mobility devices are actually less risky per km travelled than motorcycles or bicycles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Risks may also differ by the type of path travelled.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Is shifting delivery riders from PMDs to PABs going to increase or reduce overall risks?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We simply do not know and that is because the data required to estimate these effects does not exist publicly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: How much of a positive difference have active mobility devices made to our transport system and to people’s daily lives?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: LTA has been running the Household Interview Travel Survey (HITS) every four years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The last run was in 2016/2017 when active mobility device usage was just beginning to ramp up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Should there have been a special run of HITS just to cover the rapid growth in active mobility devices?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Is there a critical gap in our knowledge about active mobility device travel behaviour because we have not changed the way we run HITS, or adjusted the survey format in light of new transport trends?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Unfortunately, it is very difficult for outside researchers to contribute to this debate, because the practice is that the HITS data is kept confidential, including the survey questions themselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But did we understand that many riders had no alternative jobs or means of transport and were almost completely reliant on using PMDs on footpaths to earn a living?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, our high quality and accessible job support services are even more important.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The last Own Account Workers survey that is publicly available was conducted in 2017.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: That was when the rise in food delivery services through PMDs was just starting.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There was no indication then that thousands of Singaporeans would come to heavily depend on food delivery services to make a living.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, we believed too readily the story that such gig economy jobs are just harmless flexible side jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Now, let us consider shared mobility enterprises which the Bill also addresses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The initial heady promise of dockless shared bicycles – low-cost, efficient, first/last mile option – has given way to the realisation that these bicycle-sharing systems create huge costs for the taxpayer through indiscriminate parking and for stakeholders who are left with unrecoverable deposits or business debts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There was little regulation for months after bike-sharing systems started to appear in Singapore, perhaps because we wanted to reap the benefits without any cost to the taxpayer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: After all, LTA had called a tender in 2016 to operate a Government-subsidised bike-sharing system in the Jurong Lake District.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, why pay for bike-sharing when dockless operators were giving it to us for free?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The problem, of course, is that the costs of dockless bike-sharing were hidden.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But the answers were actually in front of us all along.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If we were prepared to introduce a Government-subsidised bike-sharing system, we would have known that bicycle-sharing systems have great difficulty recovering operating costs from user fees alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Cities sponsor such systems for the same reason that public transport is subsidised – to improve access and connectivity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is why many market observers were stunned by the rapid growth of privately funded dockless bicycle-sharing systems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: At the time, many fanciful stories were spun about how these bicycle-sharing systems would become profitable based on deposits, selling customer data and so on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Regardless, it did not matter to the operators that they lost money in the short run.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: And because it did not matter, it meant that market forces, which might otherwise have disciplined their expansion, were useless.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Market forces could not constrain the dockless bike-sharing business practice of simply dumping bicycles on the street in order to compete.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Fees and penalties could also be diverted to this fund instead of the practice under the present Bill, where they are channelled solely to the Consolidated Fund.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The purpose is just to ensure that the costs of the business model are internalised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Now, we may well find that no shared mobility enterprises will enter the market with our new regulations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We should not see that as a failure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It is actually quite unclear right now that shared mobility enterprises are even capable of being financially sustainable from user fees alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I am confident that the Government is up to the task of meeting their targets of completing the cycling infrastructure network.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But we have to be prepared for cases where what looks ideal on paper may not work in practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: After all, we have decades of experience designing for road traffic, but very little with designing for PMDs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, we should be prepared for the long haul.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: It will also not be practical to build out a cycling path network that provides standardised access everywhere.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: For example, in our private housing estates, there is generally insufficient pedestrian space available to create a cycling path.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Some HDB carpark areas also present similar challenges, as do outlying areas of Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The suggestion then is that a new classification of minor roads be designated, which could be called streets or local roads.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There would be a mandatory lower maximum speed limit for vehicles.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: There would be allowance for PMDs and active mobility on these minor roads.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Road traffic slowing features, similar to those in Silver Zones, could be introduced as standard in such areas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I want to commend AMAP for putting in unstinting efforts over the years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
