text: They are experts and stakeholders with the best of intentions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, our experience suggests we need to consider whether such advisory panels are able to draw on a sufficiently broad group of stakeholders, whether they have the resources and expertise to commission research or requisition relevant Government data, to make decisions that we can all agree are the best that could have been made at the time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: When forming such panels, we often have a practice of seeking consensus in the recommendations that are made.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I do not mean to suggest that the panel did so, and I know that there are lively debates behind the scenes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But consensus-driven thinking, unfortunately, tends to support magical policy thinking.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Who wants to spoil the general belief that all things can be worked out without too many unpleasant tradeoffs?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If we are to realise our vision of an active mobility sector that is well integrated with existing stakeholders, we need less magical thinking, and more acknowledgement of the difficult tradeoffs.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We need to reflect what we have learnt and experienced in the three years since the original Bill was passed.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The proliferation of PMDs has changed the way that we travel, work and play.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But at the same time, this has also created new problems, most vividly illustrated by the many high-profile accidents that caused personal injuries and even death.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When the PMD ban was first announced, 30 PMD riders came to my Meet-the-People Sessions to ask for help.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They were angry and they felt that their livelihood had been taken away from them without any warning.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The sentiment was more intense than a mere transport policy change.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There was that perception that their source of income has been killed and this had been enacted out of the blue.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There was no consideration for the consequences on them.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: PMD riders continued to turn up at my Meet-the-People Sessions to ask for help and this made me increasingly concerned.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It soon dawned on me that such delivery riders are gig workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They are not employees wearing uniforms of the company.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And from my interactions, I realised that the PMD controversy was just one instance of how vulnerable such gig workers are.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of them that I spoke to are doing gig work as their primary or full-time job.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They included retrenched professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) looking to earn money while searching for a new opportunity.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There were ex-prisoners who have been marginalised due to their criminal records.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of them are sole breadwinners supporting a large family.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These are vulnerable Singaporeans who need more support than they are currently getting.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They are one of many disposable contractors who have no bargaining power whatsoever against the companies that they work for.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the UK, gig economy workers are euphemistically referred to as in "precarious employment".

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If gig arrangements are here to stay, we need to give gig workers more support and more protection against their companies.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: California enacted a "Gig Worker Law" in September 2019.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They saw that Uber's market power had substantially decreased drivers' earning potential.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Similarly, our local drivers experienced the same thing during the period when Uber pulled out of the Singapore market and before Gojek came in.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Gig companies have built their businesses around avoiding the costs of employment.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Unlike traditional companies, they do not provide leave days, health insurance and other statutory benefits.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: There has been a constant complaint from traditional companies that compete against them.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: More importantly, this has created unhappiness on the ground from marginalised workers who feel unprotected.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Left unchecked, I am afraid that this issue is going to grow and fester and become another potential flashpoint.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: People feel that we are kicking them when they are down.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Even sensible policies like the PMD ban that seek to protect pedestrians have triggered strong reactions.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This suggests around 150,000 non-PMD gig workers who face different challenges and pressures.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Hence, future issues could affect even more Singaporean gig workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many other countries are doing what they can to protect their gig workers, and we need to do the same.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I believe that a solution would be to ensure that gig companies should bear their fair share of responsibility to protect their workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Other countries have introduced new legislation, but I would argue that this can be achieved under our existing legislative framework in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I was heartened to find the new section 58A of the Act mandating third-party insurance.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Businesses now need to ensure that the riders and drivers have third-party insurance before they are employed or engaged in outwork arrangements.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Those who work less than 35 hours a week should be part-time workers, and those who work more than 35 hours a week should be full-time workers.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This will protect workers by ensuring that they are provided with statutory benefits, including annual leave, sick leave, overtime pay, rest days and are paid CPF contributions, giving them the ability to save for housing, retirement and medical expenses.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Why should gig workers be excluded from such benefits?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We know that it is possible that this move will encounter pushback from the gig companies.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But our Government needs to balance creating economic growth versus safeguarding worker’s welfare.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Innovation is important but it should not be at the cost of workers' welfare.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In fact, true innovation should benefit all stakeholders, not just shareholders.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I feel strongly that such a move would help to mitigate gig workers' livelihood concerns and establish us as a caring and compassionate Government.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Additionally, we can level the playing field for other companies which are already subjected to the Employment Act.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The requirements can be phased in over time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The past five years have proven a challenge in our nation's march towards active mobility.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These measures, together, form a regulatory framework that places a premium on safety and spreads the responsibility among users and providers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, I would like to seek clarifications on both Bills and discuss the need to go further in our pursuit of active mobility.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I will first discuss my three clarifications on the Shared Mobility Enterprises (Control and Licensing) Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first clarification is about information sharing between licensees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 23 allows two licensees to enter into an information sharing agreement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Specifically, it allows them to do so for two purposes: (a) to turn away bad parkers from hiring their vehicles; and (b) to comply with directives from LTA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill’s explanatory statement states that such agreements are authorised "despite" other laws, such as the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My concern is that section 23 does not contain clear measures to deter organisations from over-sharing private user data.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, is the National Registration Identity Card (NRIC) number an appropriate datapoint to share about a bad parker?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How about passport numbers, photographs, phone numbers, email addresses, home addresses or global positioning system (GPS) locations?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The modern business collects huge amounts of private data on its customers and this data can be worth huge amounts of money.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Licensees and class licensees are mentioned in the same breath in much of the Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For some reason, class licensees are not mentioned at all in this particular section.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 13(2i) empowers LTA to collect a security deposit from licensees for the sole purpose of regulatory compliance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This means that customers who paid a deposit to shared mobility companies cannot hope to be repaid from the security deposits.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Back in early 2019, Senior Minister of State Lam Pin Min reiterated this point and suggested that disgruntled customers should sue to get their money back.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It does not seem realistic to ask hundreds or thousands of customers to go to Court to get back what might be a $50 or $100 sum.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Ministry share whether its stance has changed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why not allow the security deposits to be used to repay customers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is the principle keeping us from doing so?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, I imagine any bike-sharing operators today will have trouble persuading customers to fork up deposits.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Legislation that provides customers with some assurance might then be a win-win for consumers and businesses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 26 enables the Minister to issue a safety directive to prevent death, serious injury or serious property damage arising from the provision of any shared mobility service.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 26(2) specifies that these directives cannot be in force for longer than six months to start with and the Minister can only renew it once for no longer than six months.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In essence, a directive is capped at 12 months.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Ministry clarify what happens at the end of the 12 months if the Ministry remains concerned about the subject of the directive?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under this law, is the Minister empowered to issue a second directive?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If that is the case, what end does it serve to cap the length and frequency of the renewal?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given that these directives are used only in cases of serious concern, it would be helpful to clarify what we can expect that they do get used.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I will now discuss my two clarifications for the Active Mobility (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first clarification is on the private right of civil action.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, the current section 21 imposes obligations on riders to travel below their path's maximum speed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The new section 23C imposes duties on adult supervisors for underage riding.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Contravention of such sections are offences punishable by fines or imprisonment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, it is not clear whether the Ministry intends for breaches of duties under AMA to give rise to a private right of action.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In other words, it is not clear whether an individual injured in an accident involving a mobility device can sue another individual in tort for breach of their statutory duties under AMA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Ministry clarify whether its intention is to confer private right of civil action for the statutory duties imposed under this Act?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification is on the punishment for underage riding.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The typical sentencing consideration for young offenders is rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Imprisonment will taint a young person's record and seems like an unduly harsh punishment for underage riding of a PMD.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify the reasons for allowing imprisonment of an underage rider?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also clarify in what situations will we call for imprisonment for an underage rider?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On a similar note, the new section 23B describes conditions in which a person is deemed to have facilitated underage riding of motorised PMDs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One condition is that the person had been "reckless" as to whether their conduct would help an underage individual ride the PMD.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would it be reckless to trust a child to safeguard an unlocked e-scooter?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, the shared paths on which many young people spend their time are now the only place where PMDs can be ridden.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As we mandate good behaviours by PMD owners, we must also help them understand how to comply with the law.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To this end, it would be helpful if the Minister could describe scenarios or outline standards that exemplify "reckless" conduct.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The two Bills today deal, for the most part, with problems that have already come and gone.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Most of it is directed at PMDs and bike-sharing services, both of which are barely visible in Singapore anymore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Certainly, if these forms of mobility see a comeback, we will have built a robust regulatory framework for them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But as we spend time building the bike lanes, I hope we can start thinking about the next projects.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, how can we integrate the use of bicycles with our public transit network?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Unlike in many other major cities, you cannot bring a regular bicycle onto the bus or MRT.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even in countries with sophisticated biking infrastructure, there are many who will spend part of their commute on public transportation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We must find ways to integrate our new biking infrastructure with our world-class public transportation network.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, how can we make bike parking more secure as we discussed in the earlier Question Time?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many HDB flats have limited space and cyclists need somewhere secure to park overnight.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But how many of these spaces are unmonitored and unlocked?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Most experienced cyclists will tell you to never park your bicycle outside overnight, even at supposedly secure spots like MRT stations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What they need are affordable and accessible low-tech bicycle lockers and bicycle parking stations, ideally mapped on the MyTransport.SG app for convenience.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many cities around the world already have much success with these options.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third and lastly, how can we go beyond incremental additions to our cycling network?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My hope is that this leads the way to more ambitious plans, as we not only build in recollection of past learnings but also in anticipation of future opportunities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They were also seen as a viable solution to help Singapore transit to a car-lite society by providing commuters with an efficient means of travelling short-to-medium distances with relative ease.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is in addition to other types of mobility devices like electric-bikes, hoverboards and electric unicycles.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There were also a number of fatalities as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The amendments to the AMA are thus timely, not so much to stop the use of these devices, but to ensure that our footpaths are once again safe for the significant majority of the population.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the amendments to the AMA is to prohibit the use of mobile communications devices while operating PMDs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While comprehensive statistics on the relationship between using mobile devices when operating a PMD and the likelihood of accidents might not be fully available, we can take a leaf out from the rationale of banning the use of mobile phones while driving a car.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I thus strongly support banning the usage of mobile communications devices while operating a PMD as I believe this will minimise distractions for riders, and increase their level of attention on the road so that they are not a hazard to others and to themselves.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the topic of the minimum age of riders and competency tests, the amendments in the Bill have made some new provisions pertaining to minimum riding and supervising age.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The concept of having a minimum age is important as maturity and responsibility of PMD usage are generally correlated to the riders' age.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the devil is in the implementation details.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, while clause 23A 5(a) and 5(b) stipulate that regulations on different minimum ages could be made for different classes or descriptions of PMDs, how would the different minimum age for the different types of PMDs be determined?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Does this imply that some PMDs are deemed to be more "dangerous" than others and would, therefore, require a higher minimum age?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, if there are different minimum ages for different PMDs, would the authorities not face a challenge in implementing this on the ground as there could be various permutations of ages and device type that the regulators and enforcement officers have to deal with?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the competency theory test will certainly enhance the riders' awareness of road safety, the challenge again is in ensuring that all riders go through the test.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The new competency test would be relatively easy to enforce for new riders and those who wish to purchase PMDs as it could be stipulated that they produce their competency certificate to PMD retailers before they are allowed to purchase a PMD.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the same could not be said of existing owners of PMDs or those who co-share a PMD with their family members and friends.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How would the authorities ensure that all PMD riders are certified to be competent before they ride?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would PMD riders be required to carry with them their competency certificate at all times when they ride, just as motorists are required to have their driving licences with them while they are driving?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have some other areas of concerns, Mr Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have come across several residents who face mobility challenges, but they are not yet at a stage where they might require a motorised wheelchair specifically.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the authorities consider allowing such residents to use PMDs on footpaths if they can get themselves medically certified that they need PMDs to assist in their mobility?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In short, are we prepared to allow them to use different forms of motorised devices, other than motorised wheelchairs, to assist them in their daily commutes and movements?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Since the announcement of the ban of PMDs on footpaths in November 2019, our footpaths have, indeed, become much safer and many food delivery riders who used to ride PMDs have switched to other forms of mobility devices, such as e-bikes.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That said, there remain some deviant and recalcitrant riders who continue to ride their PMDs on footpaths in a dangerous manner.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have personally witnessed a few such cases myself.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A related issue would be how the Government intends to equip our enforcement officers with the right training to handle errant riders without compromising their own personal safety?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This was referenced earlier by Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and I am sure that many of us are familiar with the video of an enforcement officer kicking a speeding PMD rider off his device when the rider refused to stop.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should not condone the use of force by enforcement officers in the course of performing their duty, but I feel that there should be proper protocols in place for dealing with errant speeding PMD riders.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Imagine if the rider in the video was not stopped and subsequently crashed into someone and hurt them badly, or worse, even kill them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the enforcement officer have then been blamed somehow or held responsible for allowing this to happen because he was not trained to stop the errant speeding rider?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, I end my speech in support of the Bill.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There were many issues raised, reflecting the wide spectrum of views on this topic.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I will make a few general points before I start to answer the Members' questions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: First, is that despite all of the Members who spoke supporting the Bill, some of their views were entirely contradictory.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There were Members asking for increased enforcement, increased regulations and an even tighter regime than we are proposing.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And there were some Members suggesting that we are going too far.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Similarly, around the issue of children, access to different devices and so forth.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That there are contradictory views from Members reflects the difficulty in this space.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Nevertheless, all the Members supported the need for the regulatory regime that we are proposing, recognising that this approach will provide a framework for the riders, the device operators, the businesses and a coherent approach to making our paths as safe as possible for pedestrians as well as these riders.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The second general point is around walking, and I make reference to Prof Lim Sun Sun's speech as well as some of the others, such as Assoc Prof Walter Theseira.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: While we may be interested in the numbers of PMD riders, and Members have asked questions about how many there are and how many accidents and how many are compliant and so forth, we must remember that there are far, far more Singaporeans who are using that space to walk.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And actually, that is the single, biggest way in which people are closing the first-mile and last-mile gap through walking.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Walking enables them to access all the amenities of the town as well as our public transport infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, while we may or may not get every part of this regulatory approach exactly right today, we have some flexibility to adjust.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The key thing that we want to do is to ensure safety of this space for all users and the base of people walking in this space which is far, far larger.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But the ability of one PMD rider who is errant behaving poorly in this space, affects a very large number of people walking along that same path.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The third general point I want to make is that there were several comments relating to a cultural change or internalising a behavioural change.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Indeed, if we do have a culture of looking out for one another, regardless of whatever is our modality of transportation, of ensuring that we have some public spiritedness about our shared spaces, indeed, it will be a lot safer for everybody and a lot more pleasant.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is very, very difficult to do and it takes a lot of time and we may not always reach the end of the journey very easily.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have had a very strict regulatory regime for cars here in Singapore for many years.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think we would all agree that we have not reached the end of the road in establishing the kind of driving culture that we desire.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The fourth point, generally, is the issue of cycling infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There were several questions about the infrastructure plans that we have, the design, the approach that we are going to take.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These will be addressed in our Committee of Supply debate and we will have a fairly detailed discussion about it.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I do not propose to go into the details today.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If I could now move on to the specific points and questions raised by the Members.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Ang Hin Kee and Mr Ong Teng Koon brought up some issues to do with the companies' responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do agree that companies which engage riders of active mobility devices in the course of work have a social responsibility to ensure path safety both for their riders as well as the general public.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And that they must put in place the right incentive structures to encourage safe riding, as has been pointed out by a number of people.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These include sufficient time to complete their deliveries and a structure that dissuades speeding or the breaking of rules.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We strongly encourage companies to help their riders obtain personal accident insurance coverage.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Some, as has been pointed out, already do so and we hope our tripartite partners will work with us to encourage others to follow suit.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The issue of the "gig economy" and self-employed persons is significant and it is something that will cut across a number of industries and domains.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is also complex and it lies, unfortunately, well outside the scope of these Bills.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I do sympathise with Mr Ong Teng Koon's suggestions and the way in which he has highlighted the difficulties and challenges of this space.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Indeed, it does affect a number of workers which we interface with from the transport sector.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But there are many other "gig economy" and self-employed persons as well.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And I will convey his suggestions to MOM which oversees the Employment Act.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But the way in which we address this will need to be based upon our tripartite partnership.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will leverage upon this going forward and we, in the transport family, will play our part.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are measures in place to protect individual data and privacy, and the information sharing must be limited to the extent necessary to implement this ban.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For all other usage of data that is not for the purposes of this ban, PDPA will continue to apply in full force to all the operators and they are required to comply with existing data protection and privacy standards.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: LTA will assess the robustness of their systems and processes in place as part of the licence evaluation process.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There were some questions from Mr Louis Ng and Ms Anthea Ong about the issuance of safety directives by the Minister for Transport.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is intended for exceptional circumstances to allow us to tackle urgent issues of safety expeditiously.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But once it is clear what the solution is, we cannot just carry on renewing the safety directives repeatedly.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will address the problem through legislative amendments.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, that is precisely what we are doing today.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For example, today, there is a safety directive in place to disallow the usage of e-scooters for licensed device-sharing operators.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: To be clear, these safety directives are for operators, not individual hires.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the recourse for consumers who have paid deposits to shared mobility device companies.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Currently, none of the licensed device-sharing operators collect user deposits.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We shall watch and see how this space develops.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Alex Yam asked about how we would police these shared user device businesses for compliance.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The first is that the regular ground enforcement, of course, will pick up issues of non-compliance when the customers of these businesses transgress.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Operators, as part of their licensing process, will be required to demonstrate that they have processes in place to ensure that the users that they hired out their vehicles to, for example, have the appropriate test certificate, and this will include tourists.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The operational details of how these tests will be administered both to people who have devices and new device owners and tourists, will need to be worked out.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will make some announcements in due course.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But, importantly, we will have to work with the operators and businesses to make sure that this is something effective.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But we intend for this to cover all riders.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If I could move to the personal mobility aids that Mr Darryl David, in particular, brought up.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The ban of motorised PMDs on footpaths, let me state once again, does not apply to PMAs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Such PMAs do not only include motorised wheelchairs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There are also other types of devices, such as mobility scooters and so forth.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, to the Member's specific question, if there are individuals with walking difficulties, there are other devices which perhaps, for want of a better word, are not as "medicalised" as a motorised wheelchair that may be more suitable for someone who perhaps is not in such a serious condition.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And it will be more appropriate for them to use such a device, rather than to have a very, very different process where the individuals then requires a waiver for something like an e-scooter.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And that is the way that we will try to help these individuals.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked several questions about PABs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The aim is to ensure that there are different options available and that device users can choose the best mode of transport based on their needs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, the motorised PMD users can continue to ride on cycling paths or can switch to bicycles if they want to ride on footpaths.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For this process to work, there has to be some ability for individual users to address their own level of comfort, their need for speed, as it were, and how they will make the choice between a PAB, a bicycle or a PMD.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But whatever it is, we have to have a robust framework to ensure safety.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: On the roads, the PABs will be regulated and already currently are regulated by LTA and the Traffic Police (TP).

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do not allow underage riding on PABs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is no opportunity for the similar type of adult supervision of an underage rider.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And when riding on roads, all PAB riders must comply with road traffic regulations, such as travelling in the direction of traffic, wearing helmets and riding safely.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We also regulate the PAB devices in the same way we have a framework for the devices, the riders as well as businesses.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: All PABs must be registered and only the LTA-approved models are allowed to be used in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The restrictions on these devices prevent sudden accelerations and increases the predictability of a PAB rider to other road motorists.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They also have to comply with the device safety standard European Commission EN15194 for electrical and fire safety.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will continue to monitor the use of PABs and take further steps if necessary.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I would point out one issue brought up by Mr Alex Yam.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, there will be a one-year period for that turnover.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If I may now move to the issue of insurance.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This was brought up by Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, Mr Alex Yam, Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Louis Ng.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ideally, yes, all users should have some form of insurance covering the rider himself and any victim.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is a practical problem, however – there are few active mobility-related insurance products available today.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do want to progress in this direction, provide a critical mass of demand and allow the insurance industry to develop more affordable and comprehensive products.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will continue to work with AMAP and the insurance industry.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But in the meantime, we strongly encourage all active mobility device riders to purchase such insurance to protect themselves from claims.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira has several suggestions which we will study in some detail and I think they are very reasonable ones, indeed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked about the balance between the business and employer.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Potentially, it could be either, but the business would need to ensure that the employee or the rider, if the business is hiring the device out, has evidence of this third-party liability insurance if they are not themselves providing it.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the courses of action.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have no intention to introduce new courses of action beyond what is available today.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Today, victims of accidents on public paths can seek compensation from the rider for injury and losses suffered through civil proceedings, settlements and other private arrangements.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I encourage all owners of a non-UL2272-certified and a non-registered PMD to dispose of that PMD before the end of March 2020.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Currently, that disposal does not cost the rider or the owner anything.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That is almost certainly going to change and incur some fee after the end of March.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Darryl David, Mr Alex Yam and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked about the testing regime.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: How we will operationalise this theory test and enforcement, we are currently working out these operational details and we will release more information once we have worked this through with the operators.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will continue to ramp up enforcement efforts to ensure compliance to our rules.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: LTA has caught more than 130 e-scooter riders since 1 January 2020 for violating the footpath ban.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will continue this approach to deter errant riding and ensure safety.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There have been suggestions for our enforcement officers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Indeed, we will continue to train them and equip them to handle different scenarios through more robust rules of engagement and better training.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This includes strategies to tackle cases, such as evasive riders.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I am sure the Members appreciate that I am not going through the specifics of our enforcement strategy and tactics because we do wish them to be as effective as possible.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But it does include the further use of technology, as suggested, including, for example, mobile closed-circuit television (CCTV) cameras.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah has suggested that we have an upper age limit for seniors.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For people who have difficulty walking, we have made provisions for PMAs to be used.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We would encourage those seniors who have difficulty with their mobility and need assistance and who may have the sort of healthcare problems that Er Dr Lee Bee Wah had brought up, to use a PMA which are safer and more stable, and not a PMD.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But if I may move to underage riding, the minimum riding age would be introduced for e-scooters as a subset of motorised PMDs first.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Darryl David asked about the powers under section 23A allowing the prescription of different minimum ages for different classes of PMDs.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is really to give us some flexibility because we cannot anticipate the new types of devices that may arise in the future.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It allows us at the time to put in the appropriate regulations where necessary.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is something that has been called for repeatedly by many Singaporeans and AMAP as well, and we have fixed it at 16.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Many families enjoy outings using these devices together and we want to allow for this.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Hence, the idea of a supervising adult for the underage rider.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do not want to be overly prescriptive about what the supervising adult must do.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Sensible measures include staying close to the young rider, maintaining a proper line of sight to the rider, knowing and educating the rider of the appropriate rules and regulations, and taking appropriate measures to stop the rider if they are committing an offence or may get into an accident.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are developing guidelines to educate these supervising adults on how to properly supervise the underage rider.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ms Anthea Ong and Mr Louis Ng asked about the penalties for the underage rider.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If I can reiterate what I said in my opening speech, these penalties only provide the limit of the possible sentence.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Courts retain the discretion to consider the circumstances of the case, including the age of the individual and the laws on sentencing of young offenders found in the Children and Young Persons Act (CYPA), in deciding the actual punishment to mete out.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Regarding the question from Mr Louis Ng about section 23B of the Active Mobility Bill which introduces an offence of inviting, allowing or facilitating underage riding of devices, the principle is to ensure that device owners or device-sharing operators take responsibility for the use of their devices, including ensuring that the devices are not used by an underage individual.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This could include putting in place measures to check the age of customers hiring the devices or individuals who are borrowing the device or locking the device so that it is only available for one's own use.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Where individuals are concerned, they should make sure that the device is not readily accessed by underage individuals.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Dennis Tan had asked about an issue associated with underage riding and the liability of the rider versus the supervisor.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As Members have noted, there have been many calls to improve public path safety as well as fire safety arising from use of these devices.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have taken these concerns very seriously and which is why my colleague Senior Minister of State Lam Pin Min delivered the Statement on PMDs in August to address these concerns and established that we would have to tighten our regime if the situation did not improve.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And the situation did not improve over a number of months.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Accidents continue to rise in number and severity.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We had to move decisively in order to prevent more deaths and more accidents.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We were mindful of the impact the move would have on e-scooter users, especially for those who had come to rely on it for their livelihoods.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That was why we had provided a two-month advisory period – it is not an overnight ban – a two-month advisory period and worked closely with food delivery companies, the Labour Movement and other partners to support food delivery riders in the transition.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This strong tripartite collaboration enabled us to launch a Transition Assistance Package, a comprehensive approach to help these food delivery riders.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We were able to do this four days after announcing the ban.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are heartened that the three food delivery companies stepped up to co-fund with the Government the e-scooter Trade-in Grant to help the riders transition to other devices.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Ang Hin Kee had some suggestions to build on NTUC’s existing training modules when LTA implements the mandatory theory test requirements.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These are good suggestions and we will leverage our good relationship with NTUC to see how we can best operationalise this.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: To achieve this, we need the right infrastructure and the right regulatory approach.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The ideal for infrastructure is segregation – keeping different groups of users – footpaths for pedestrians and slow-moving devices like bicycles and PMAs; roads for motor vehicles; and cycling paths for devices of intermediate speeds, such as motorised PMDs and PABs – all separate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Today, we have an extensive network of footpaths and roads.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We had previously announced that we will extend the cycling path network from 440 km to 750 km by 2025 and 1,300 km by 2030.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will elaborate on these plans at the Committee of Supply debate next month.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Going forward, we will continue to strike a delicate balance in ensuring Singaporeans can reap the benefits of active mobility, ensuring public safety and enabling business innovation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Where possible, we will try our best to anticipate the changes and put in place the necessary frameworks ahead of time.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But it is not possible to predict all the ways that users, retailers and device operators will change their behaviour or find ways to circumvent our regulations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Rather than saying no to all innovations because of this, we want to continue to facilitate in a measured manner where there are clear benefits.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And where we cannot anticipate, we will consult deeply, study the matter and move decisively to address the issues and challenges as they occur.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will continue to consult widely and engage regularly, to ensure that our policies remain relevant to Singapore, Singaporeans and their aspirations – not just on active mobility, but in general.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I would finally like to express my appreciation for the many stakeholders who have made these Bills possible – AMAP members, the tripartite partners, the industry stakeholders, members of the public who provided views and suggestions as part of the AMAP consultation process and, of course, Members of the House for their support of the Bill.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: I think the Senior Minister of State did not address the topic on drunk riding.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: The second question: for those cyclists that are using the road, when they cycle against the traffic, is it an offence?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: If yes, what are the measures to be taken?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: I think more education needs to be carried out.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: I think many of them are not aware that actually it is an offence.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: And I see that quite often in, for example, Serangoon Gardens where there are a lot of one-way road and then I see cyclists in the opposite direction.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Indeed, the issues that Er Dr Lee Bee Wah brought up are today covered under the Road Traffic Act.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is easier said than done and we need a combination of enforcement and education, as the Member has pointed out.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I appreciate the Senior Minister of State's clarification that the Courts would obviously make the decision and make reference to CYPA.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: But it still does not discount the fact that the children will, first, be charged.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: And I just want to bring to attention that many of the children in low-income families, including in rental flat communities, they use PMDs as a primary form of their transport.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Should we actually put them through that without considering at least some form of warning?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I am not saying they should not be penalised if they are actually errant.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I am saying that getting them charged and then getting them directly to the Courts really seem aggressive, particularly for underage riders.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: So, will the Senior Minister of State share if he will consider at least some warning or some reformative training before we get to exercise charging them in the Courts?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I take it that Ms Anthea Ong has no objection for there to be a minimum age of riding.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I am trying to understand whether the Member is objecting to the fact that there should be a minimum age of riding or does she agree that there should be a minimum age.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: No, I am not disputing there should be a minimum age.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: I am saying that it is still very aggressive.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Because 16 is seen, in CYPA, as still a child.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think the officer picking up the transgression needs to be able to understand that they have to deal with these two scenarios differently, as do the agencies and subsequently the Courts.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think to guarantee that every case is dealt with exactly the same way would be an inappropriate commitment at this point in time.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: Can I then ask what are we planning to do in terms of getting these new laws and regulations to our vulnerable communities and all the children to make sure that they understand this is going to be in place?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think we have to be quite clear about the perspective here.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Ms Anthea Ong has brought up the vulnerable, low-income many, many times.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The most important way for all our communities, including the vulnerable and low-income, to get around is by walking and using public transport, and they close the last-mile gap, not through a PMD, but through many other different means.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have to have our priority in ensuring the safety of that space.
